inline.s: Here we can see all the more clearly the importance of a person’s faith, the importance of conviction. A person who believes in Buddhism will never smoke; even if he once smoked, he will give it up entirely. One whose convictions are distorted cannot generate strength within himself to bring himself happiness, and so must rely on smoking a few harmful cigarettes to “produce” happiness — what does that amount to?

It is the same with drinking. Drinking harms the liver and can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer, yet one whose convictions are wrong still drinks, making drinking the sole joy of life without regard for the consequences.
Drink is not the true cause of illness, because drink does not run into a person’s mouth by itself. Why does one drink? Why can one not stop drinking? That is the true cause.
A person who believes in Buddhism will never drink.

Human life is long or short, and the length has its own “cause.” Since in this world there are people who live past a hundred, to a hundred and ten or a hundred and fifteen years, and who yet live healthily and joyfully, this can prove that humans are a temporary union of the four great elements — earth, water, fire, and wind. As long as the four elements are in harmony, one need not be ill, need not die young, need not have a short life.
What others can accomplish, we too should be able to accomplish.
The mistaken convictions and mistaken conduct of the past can still be corrected today — it is not too late.
Practicing according to the Buddha’s instruction: precepts, meditation, and wisdom.
Not only do we live in health, we can also attain nirvāṇa and be liberated from the cycle of birth and death!
Each of us has a story — a true story, one lived through in person. I too have my story. Though the past has become the past, when I recall it, it still stands before my eyes, vivid as if present.

The experiences of a life are the record of our being, and are useful material. This material may serve as a reference for oneself and for others as well. Precisely because my story holds blood and tears, sorrow and despair — and because I endured them all — I am willing to make it public.

The Buddha said: life is good. Indeed, in a life of suffering we have only to follow the Buddha’s instruction, to plant good causes as much as we can, to clear away the bitter fruits, and to summon our willpower and press forward. The road ahead may be winding and hard, but it is better than retreating or standing still. Belief in the Buddha helps the mind and helps the body — the facts are before our eyes to prove it.
May my story give you insight; may the Buddha’s teaching give you guidance.
When I was still a little girl of eighteen months, my parents divorced.

Because of my tender age I did not know how great an effect this had on me, but my mother had to go out to work as a hired hand in another’s household. She sent me to a strange place, to be cared for by strangers. There I cried for three weeks without stopping, so that those caring for me were at a loss and did not know what to do. My mother could only take me home and think of some other way.
As a single parent she raised me, and I came to love and honor her. Yet in the end she could not devote herself wholly to caring for me, and this is what I grieve over deeply.

I never knew the reason my mother married my stepfather. Was it because she loved him, or because she wanted to give her child a happy home? In any case, it was not a wise move. My stepfather had been raised in a traditional German family and had a very brutal nature; in the way he treated us he could not free himself of that brutal habit.
My mother later became pregnant with my younger sister. By the 1930s the world economy was in depression, and our family became an even more brutal and darker home. I was only five years old then.

As the saying goes, misfortunes never come singly. Just when I was five years old, a neighbor of ours, an old drunkard, raped me. I clearly remember the doctor examining me, and I remember that in the courtroom I was the victim. Though the man was punished by the law and sentenced to fifteen years in prison, I was endlessly blamed: “It was all your fault!”
Therefore for many years I worried, fearing that once the man finished his sentence and left prison, he would come to take revenge on me for having put him there.
Most of my childhood I endured physical and sexual abuse. My self-esteem grew lower day by day; nothing had a good effect on me, and I felt that even the outside world was a vicious cycle.

When I was in the fourth grade, one incident can show what my life was like then. Our school held a party and there were many cakes to be given out to the students. Except for me, the children of the school all came from comfortable middle-class families; by contrast my clothing was the shabbiest. I wore a ragged haircut, long black shoes, and the smell of raw garlic in my mouth — a smell that came from my being forced every day to eat raw garlic “to keep away parasites.”

We never had cake at home, because we simply could not afford it. An old woman nearby took pity on me and gave me ten cents every week; and on my birthday she would give me a dollar. But the ten cents were all used for household expenses, and the dollar bought the underwear I wore that year.

That day the school party handed out many cakes. The children who ate cake every day each received two or three pieces; but when the teacher came to me — and of course I was last in line — she gave me not a single piece, because they had all been given to the other classmates.

I was very sad at the time, but now I clearly understand that it was because I then presented myself at school as worthless, undeserving of any reward, that I was placed last in line and could not get even a piece of cake. It was entirely that I made myself disagreeable; they were only reflecting their displeasure with me.

When I was fifteen, my understanding had awakened and I could no longer endure the sexual abuse, so I ran away from school and home. I found a job as a waitress in a restaurant. Although the work was hard, it was far easier than all the physical labor I had done at home. Because I had developed not a shred of self-esteem, I was famished for love and care, to the point that I would give my body to anyone who showed me concern.
Just after my sixteenth birthday, I gave birth to a baby girl.

I felt I had no ability to care for her, so I found her a good, loving home — a couple without children who greatly hoped for a baby. I went to live in their home for four months before giving birth, then went to the hospital to deliver, and the child took their name from birth.

Because circumstances were thus, I could not experience any of the joy of being a mother; instead there was only a sense of loss, along with guilt and shame. Those were days filled to the extreme with shame, and I only wished to get through them as quickly as possible. All I remember of my baby girl is her big toe, which was like mine — quite unusual. If we ever meet again, I think I would recognize her just by seeing her big toe.

When the baby was five days old, I left. I returned home, and my mother no longer wished to endure the abuse of her second husband, so I said to her: “Let us go together. You need not suffer all this any longer; I will take you away from here.”
She came with me, leaving behind my ten-year-old sister, who had always been loved by her father.

I helped my mother find a cleaning job at a small inn and settled her in a place where she could feel free and comfortable. Feeling my duty was done, I went with a girlfriend to Chicago. At first I intended to stay only a month, but in the end I went and stayed thirty years, and never once returned.

In those early days of mine, in my childhood, I experienced much violence; and because I later developed poorly and felt myself worthless, I attracted only men who treated me badly, even beating me. If I had gone through the rest of my life endlessly resenting and blaming men without knowing how to change myself, I might still be just as miserable to this day. But after much positive work and experience, my self-esteem grew, and that kind of bad man at last gradually left my life.

In the past I believed deep in my subconscious that I was only meant to be abused, so even men whose conduct was very bad I still accepted. If my own thinking had not been wrong, I would not have drawn such men to me. Now, any man who abuses women has nothing to do with me. There is no longer any mutual attraction between us.

In Chicago I at first did only menial work. After a few years I went to New York and was fortunate enough to become a high-fashion model. But being a model for those famous fashion designers did not help me gain much self-esteem; rather it gave me all the more chances to find fault with myself, and I refused to admit that I was beautiful.

I kept working in the fashion world. Many years later I married an English gentleman of excellent character and high education. We traveled all over the world, met famous people, and even dined at the White House.
Though I was a fashion model and had married such a good man, my self-esteem was still very low.

After fourteen years of marriage, I had just begun to believe that all that was good could last unchanged, when one day he suddenly announced that he had fallen in love with someone else and was preparing to end our marriage. At that time my suffering truly defies description.

But time passed day by day and I went on living; then I began to feel my life changing. A fortune-teller predicted that in autumn a small thing would happen, and that this small thing could greatly transform my life. I paid no attention to such predictions. A few months later autumn came, and quite by chance I attended a gathering of the “Religious Science Association” held in New York City. Everything was quite unfamiliar to me, yet within me there was a feeling urging me to “listen with care.” I therefore listened with care, and joined the gatherings and study courses they held every Sunday. The Buddhist courses gave me the greatest interest and inspiration.

After this, the world of fashion and adornment gradually lost its hold on my interest; I wondered how many more years I could go on concerning myself with my waistline and the shape of my eyebrows. From an ignoramus who had not finished middle school, I became an eager student, reading book after book on religion and healing. The “Religious Science” center became my new home. Though most of my life went on as before, all this new learning began to take up more and more of my time.
